closing_note.summary: 80-year-old woman with treated non-Hodgkin lymphoma, HFpEF, hypertension and coronary disease admitted after presyncopal lightheadedness, brief loss of consciousness and rapid spontaneous recovery. Admission BP 86/58 mmHg with bilateral pitting oedema and fatigue. Cardiac evaluation for arrhythmia and structural disease was unrevealing; echocardiography showed EF 60–65%, normal LV thickness, trivial regurgitation. Admission labs: urine protein 3+, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 45 mg/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, UPCR 10 g/g. She was diagnosed with adrenal insufficiency during admission and treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; confirmatory cortisol/ACTH values, doses and timing are not supplied. Serum free light chains: lambda 131 mg/L, kappa 14.41 mg/L, ratio 0.11; immunofixation shows IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy. Nephrotic syndrome of uncertain cause; outpatient renal biopsy scheduled. Prioritised explanations: (1) Monoclonal-protein–related renal disease (e.g., amyloid or light-chain/cryoglobulin-mediated glomerular injury) associated with IgM lambda gammopathy and lambda excess — plausible given heavy new proteinuria, but unproven without tissue. (2) Lymphoma-associated or paraneoplastic glomerulopathy — possible, but lymphoma subtype and staging are not established here. (3) Adrenal insufficiency with hypotension contributing to syncope and possibly to pre-renal creatinine rise — supported by treatment given, but confirmatory testing is unreported and it does not explain proteinuria. Syncope itself is most consistent with transient hypoperfusion given rapid recovery and negative cardiac work-up. Next steps: proceed with the scheduled renal biopsy, obtain cortisol/ACTH confirmation and repeat vitals/creatinine, and clarify lymphoma classification.
